solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: (& 10ac.) "Famously ineffective session of MPs" (Cyclops' cryptic rendering of 'ear implant')

parts.note: surface reading: a notoriously useless sitting of the Commons from history
setter's reading: the answer is itself a clue, with a scrambling word followed by letters that rearrange to give the phrase in quotes

explanation.surface: A note on a notoriously useless sitting of Parliament, with the setter boasting of a medical-sounding pun.
explanation.walkthrough: The Addled Parliament of 1614 passed no legislation. Read as a clue, ADDLED signals a rearrangement and PARLIAMENT rearranges to EAR IMPLANT, which is the setter's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1614 assembly under James I sat for weeks and enacted nothing, earning this historical nickname for futility.

clue.text: see 27ac.
Poetically emotional, disgustingly rich element

indicators.note: an element is a component part, so the letters are a part of the neighbouring words

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone complaining that a poem has a sickly, over-rich ingredient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element' reads like a chemical or ingredient, but it signals that the answer sits inside disgustingLY RICh.
explanation.definitionFit: Lyric poetry expresses personal feelings, so the adjective describes verse that conveys strong private feeling.

clue.text: Maybe I'd comply with American premier's tactfulness

indicators.note: 'maybe' says the letters are only one possible arrangement, so they can be put in another order
a premier is the first in rank, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted

parts.note: taken as written
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone musing that they might go along with a US president's smooth manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American premier' suggests the US president; it is just the letter A, which joins I'D COMPLY in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Diplomacy, in its everyday sense, is skill at handling people delicately, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Those on lowest income trashed by Toffs Row

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and thrown about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The poor are being done down by a row of posh people, perhaps the Tory front bench.
explanation.walkthrough: Toffs are upper-class people in British slang; their letters rearrange into the phrase for the poorest.
explanation.definitionFit: The worst off in society are the people with the least money, so the phrase names the lowest earners.

clue.text: Line up your quaint VIP

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a line of things is a row
thy is the old-fashioned form of 'your'

explanation.surface: An instruction to queue up behind some old-fashioned dignitary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quaint' tells you to use the archaic word for 'your', which is THY.
explanation.definitionFit: A worthy, as a noun, is a notable or important person, often said slightly mockingly of local bigwigs.

clue.text: Remains, as grizzlies head off?

indicators.note: with the head taken off, a word loses its first letter

parts.note: bruin is a traditional name for a bear, and grizzlies are bears

explanation.surface: A grim picture of what is left after bears have been decapitated.
explanation.walkthrough: Bruin is the folk-tale name for a bear; take off its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruins are what is left of a destroyed building, so they are the leftover traces of something.

clue.text: Prison sentence comes before hearing? That puts you up against the clock

definitions.text: That puts you up against the clock

indicators.note: to come before is to be placed ahead, so one piece is written first and the next follows

parts.note: doing time is serving a prison sentence
a court hearing of a case

explanation.surface: The legal process in the wrong order, with sentencing before the case is heard.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a legal reading, but the definition is from sport, such as cycling.
explanation.definitionFit: In a time trial each competitor races alone and the result depends only on the stopwatch reading.

clue.text: At last Corbyn has cut intended funds

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so one piece is driven into the other

parts.note: your intended is the person you are engaged to marry

indicators.note: 'at last' points to the final position, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of the name

explanation.surface: Jeremy Corbyn, Labour leader, finally slashing the money that had been earmarked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intended' looks like an adjective qualifying funds, but it is a noun: a fiancé.
explanation.definitionFit: Finance can mean money or resources available for spending, so it serves as a synonym for funding.

clue.text: Bath wedged against your end? Scrap?

parts.note: Bath is a spa town, and a bath can be a spa

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A bathtub jammed against someone's bottom, then a question of whether to throw it out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a verb meaning discard, but here it means a fight; 'end' is the bottom in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to fight or argue, and a scrap is a fight, so both are verbs for squabbling.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Ultimately, Trump displays crazy, pathetic, mammoth ego — scary picture!

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means in the end, so the closing letter of each word is taken

parts.words: Trump displays crazy, pathetic, mammoth ego
parts.note: final letters of the six words

explanation.surface: A rant about Trump's vast, unhinged ego, which is frightening to see.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites calling Trump a name; the answer is the name of a film, made of the last letters of the six words before the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: Psycho is Hitchcock's 1960 horror film, and picture is an older word for a movie, so it is an example.

clue.text: Male model with fantastic tan? Not how Trump comes across

parts.note: the male pronoun

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or bizarre, so the letters take an odd new form

parts.note: to model for an artist is to sit
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dig at Trump's famously orange tan, painting him as a vain male model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a noun but is the verb, as when one poses for a portrait. The definition is the opposite of Trump's brash manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump is famously brash and self-assured, so a word for tentative or wavering describes what he is not.

clue.text: Stacks of cash over at retail chain — it's only temporary

indicators.note: turned over means flipped round, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: pots of money means large amounts of it
Gap is a clothing store chain

explanation.surface: Big profits at a high-street chain are only a passing phase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as 'finished at', but it turns the money word round.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopgap is a makeshift measure used until something better arrives, so it lasts only a while.

clue.text: "Fat belly on tough old bird": hardly high literature

parts.note: a pot belly is a round paunch
a boiler is an old chicken fit only for boiling; also a rude slang word for an unattractive older woman

explanation.surface: A quoted put-down of a pulp novel's plot, followed by a sniffy literary verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted line sounds like an insult about a person, but it splits into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A potboiler is a novel churned out quickly to make money, the opposite of serious literary fiction.

clue.text: Old-fashioned court twerp inhaling glue

indicators.note: to inhale is to take in, so one piece is drawn inside the other

parts.note: a twerp is a fool, and so is an ass
size is a gluey substance used to seal paper or plaster

explanation.surface: A fool sniffing glue in some antique court of law.
explanation.walkthrough: The glue word sits between the two S's of the fool word; size is a sealant painters and decorators use.
explanation.definitionFit: The assizes were periodic county courts in England and Wales, abolished in 1972, hence a dated name.

clue.text: Don't attack Lebanese city's central expansion

parts.note: to spare someone is to refrain from harming them
Tyre is an ancient port city in Lebanon

explanation.surface: A plea not to strike a Lebanese city as it grows from its centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central expansion' reads like urban sprawl; it is a waistline.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare tyre is a jocular idiom for a roll of fat round the waist, which is growth in the middle.

clue.text: Stop reading our mag, Kip!

parts.note: to stop or close
the setter's magazine is Private Eye

explanation.surface: A reader being told to put down the magazine and go to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: This puzzle appears in Private Eye, so 'our mag' is EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Kip is British slang for a nap or sleep, and shut-eye is another informal word for the same.

clue.text: Charity gets together with love in shack

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so these pieces go within another

parts.note: a shack is a rough hut
'and' joins things together
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A charity's love-in, bringing people together in a humble shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Together with' is simply AND; with O for love it goes inside the shack word.
explanation.definitionFit: A handout is money or goods given free to those in need, which is what charity provides.

clue.text: Rather big feature of Stalin: holding back poor

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: Stalin's moustache; tash is British slang for a moustache

indicators.note: going back means going in the opposite direction, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: in poor health

explanation.surface: Stalin's grand persona, with the regime keeping the poor down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding back poor' sounds like oppression; it is a container plus a reversal. Stalin's famous feature was his moustache, a 'tash' in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish means somewhat, so somewhat tall is moderately big in height.

clue.text: Make sure your partner gets enough fist action in for example?

definitions.text: Make sure your partner gets enough
definitions.note: the whole phrase describes the verb

indicators.note: being in something means being placed inside it

parts.note: say is used to introduce an example

indicators.note: action implies movement, so these letters are set moving into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky piece of bedroom advice about keeping a partner contented.
explanation.walkthrough: The innuendo distracts: 'for example' is the stock phrase used when introducing an instance, and 'action' is the scrambling signal, not part of the sex joke.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy someone is to meet their needs or desires fully, so they have had as much as they want.

clue.text: Very dull dirty dog put in enclosure

indicators.note: putting something in means placing it inside, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs

indicators.note: something dirty is messed up, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boring, mucky hound being shut in a pen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dirty' reads as describing the dog, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Stodgy, said of writing or people, means heavy and tedious, much like stodgy food sits heavily.

clue.text: Disrespectful, having capsized off the South coast?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rude and lacking respect

definitions.text: having capsized off the South coast?
definitions.note: a cryptic phrase read as two words
definitions.meaning: second meaning: where a boat that overturned off Hampshire might be, split into two words

explanation.surface: A rude remark about someone whose boat overturned off the English south coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as IN SOLENT: the Solent is the strait between the Isle of Wight and Hampshire, so a capsized boat might be lying there.
explanation.definitionFit: Insolent means rude and showing contempt, a close synonym of disrespectful in ordinary usage.

clue.text: Lassitude at the heart of drunken nuisance

indicators.note: the heart is the inner part, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Weariness is what lies behind someone being a drunken pest.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are inside drunkEN NUIsance.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is listless boredom and weariness, which is what lassitude means too.

clue.text: Turn on old partner wanting sex in church

parts.note: a former spouse or lover

indicators.note: something in another is placed inside it

parts.note: the Church of England
'it' is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A former lover craving sex in a church, which is a scandalous scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn on' looks like 'betray' in this surface, but it means arouse. IT for sex and CE for the Church of England are standard.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn someone on is to arouse them, especially sexually, and excite has that same meaning.

clue.text: Big shot wants ad removed in stupid debacle

indicators.note: something stupid is senseless, so the letters lose their sensible order
removed means taken away, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written
these two letters are taken away

explanation.surface: A star demanding an advert be pulled in the middle of a fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: Take A and D out of DEBACLE and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A big shot is an important or famous person, and a celeb is a slang term for a celebrity.

clue.text: Artfully play God, holding nothing back — maybe the one that made Brexit a reality?

definitions.text: maybe the one that made Brexit a reality

indicators.note: going back means running the other way, so the letters are reversed
to hold is to keep within, so the outer letters enclose another piece
done artfully means cleverly worked, so the letters are crafted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
nil is zero

explanation.surface: A wry take on the 2016 Brexit referendum as an exercise in playing God.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged PLAY GOD wraps round NIL reversed. 'Maybe' marks the definition as one example, the referendum vote of 23 June 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: Brexit followed the vote held on referendum day in June 2016, an example of a day when electors cast ballots.

clue.text: (& 2dn.) Abandoned lay: the failed would-be MP's forfeit

parts.note: an abandoned cause is one given up and no longer to be won
to lay down something

explanation.surface: A love affair dropped by a candidate who lost the election and paid the price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay' suggests a sexual partner; it is the verb meaning to put down. UK election candidates pay £500, kept if they win under 5% of the vote.
explanation.definitionFit: A British parliamentary candidate who polls under five percent forfeits the £500 stake paid when standing.

clue.text: "One can't go on longer than this": Brenda coming to end of reign, overwhelmed by it, yet perverse

definitions.text: One can't go on longer than this

indicators.note: to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so this piece is surrounded
perverse means contrary or twisted, so the letters go a different way

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only the closing letter is taken
to come to something is to join it, so these pieces sit next to each other

parts.note: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the late Queen, whose cipher was ER
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: The Queen, nearing the end of her reign, saying in royal style that she can go on no longer.
explanation.walkthrough: ER plus the last letter of 'reign' goes inside a rearranged IT YET. 'One' reads as royal speech but is just a generic person.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternity is endless time, so nothing can last beyond it; the definition is a playful description.

clue.text: Without me member, lost way, ultimately, love — and that's just the beginning

indicators.note: something lost is confused and astray, so the letters wander into another order
without means lacking, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
these two letters are removed

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means at the end, so only the closing letter is used

parts.note: final letter of the word
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A lament about a lost member and lost love, and that being only the start of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ME from MEMBER, scramble the rest, then add the last letter of 'way' and O for love.
explanation.definitionFit: An embryo is the earliest stage of an organism's development, so it is a beginning of life.
